extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishing production staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the structure, placement, formatting, and metadata of book and journal elements (front matter, back matter, subheads, covers, metadata, abstracts, pagination, and related production conventions). Useful for preparing manuscripts and for editorial/production decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion placement and titling
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion may assume the significance and proportions of a final chapter, with or without a chapter number; authors should consider using a more descriptive title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conclusion may begin recto or verso; for a book divided into parts it must begin recto so it does not appear to belong only to the final part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue or afterword placement and style
rubrics_metrics.description: An epilogue or afterword is a comparatively brief section that comments on the text or brings a narrative up to date; when added to a new edition and written by a different author it is usually called an afterword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally follows any conclusion and may begin recto or verso; for a book divided into parts or an afterword added to a new edition it should usually begin recto; set in same size and style of type as the rest of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subhead wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Subheads within a chapter should be short and meaningful and, like chapter titles, parallel in structure and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first sentence of text following a subhead should not refer syntactically to the subhead; repeat words where necessary to maintain clarity (examples shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subhead levels and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works need only one level of subhead; scientific or technical works may require further subdivision into A-, B-, C-levels, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the most complicated works need more than three levels; the number of levels may vary by chapter; when subdividing, ideally provide at least two subsections (e.g., two or more A-level subheads in a chapter or two or more B-level subheads under an A-level), though occasional single subdivisions are acceptable for emphasis or specialized sections (e.g., chapter endnotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Run-in subhead formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: The lowest-level subhead may be run in at the beginning of a paragraph and followed by a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run-in subheads are usually set in italics or boldface and capitalized sentence-style; levels are generally differentiated by type style and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered subheads and multilevel numeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless sections are cited elsewhere, numbers are usually unnecessary for subheads; in scientific and technical works numbering sections/subsections provides easy reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common multilevel numbering uses chapter.section.subsection (e.g., 4.12.3). The manual's system uses chapter number followed by paragraph number; multiple numeration may also be used for illustrations, tables, and equations. Note: multiple numeration using periods is not decimal fractions (4.9 then 4.10 is normal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamental or typographic breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a break stronger than a paragraph but weaker than a subhead is required, use asterisks, a type ornament, or a blank line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blank lines can be missed at page bottoms and in reflowable electronic text; differentiate the first few words after the break (e.g., small caps) or adopt another consistent signaling strategy across all publication formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix purpose and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: An appendix may include explanations, elaborations, texts of documents, long lists, questionnaires, charts or tables that are helpful but not essential to the main text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendixes usually follow the last book chapter, but an appendix essential to a chapter may appear at the end of that chapter introduced by an A-level subhead; in multiauthor books appendixes must follow the chapter they pertain to; designate multiple appendixes by numbers or letters and give each a title; appendixes may be set in same or smaller type size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix as repository prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: An appendix should not be a repository for odds and ends the author couldn't work into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put relevant but unwieldy or expensive-to-print material on the publisher’s website when appropriate (more common with journals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A chronological list of events may be useful and can appear in the back matter under its own heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If essential to understanding the narrative, place it in the front matter immediately before the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary ordering and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A glossary lists words to be defined alphabetically, each on a separate line followed by a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A glossary usually precedes the notes and bibliography/reference list but may follow the notes; a glossary of terms not appearing in the text may be included as an appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endnotes placement and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Endnotes (headed 'Notes') follow appendix material and precede the bibliography or reference list; notes to each chapter are introduced by a subhead indicating the chapter number and often the chapter title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Running heads for endnotes should identify the pages/chapters the notes apply to; endnotes are normally set smaller than text but larger than footnotes; in multiauthor books, place notes at the ends of chapters; notes to tables/data may remain with the appendix; see specific sections for unnumbered notes or notes keyed to line/page numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of contributors placement and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of contributors (headed 'Contributors') is appropriate for multiauthor works where only the volume editor’s name appears on the title page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred location is back matter immediately before the index; arrange names alphabetically by last name but not inverted (e.g., 'Aiden A. Author', not 'Author, Aiden A.'); include brief biographical notes, affiliations, and contact information if authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index placement and format
rubrics_metrics.description: The index (or first of several indexes) begins on a recto; in printed books indexes are normally set two columns per page and in smaller type than the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In books with both name and subject indexes, the name index should precede the subject index; see chapter on indexing for full discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical note consistency and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief biographical note on the author(s) lists previous publications and relevant affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical notes may appear in back matter (usually final element), front matter, or on the back cover/inside flap per publisher preference; if present in more than one place, details (if not wording) must be consistent; Chicago prefers back cover/inside flap over the copyright page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colophon usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A colophon is an inscription including facts of production that may appear as the last page of a specially designed/produced book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colophon placement is optional and used for specially produced books; note alternate meanings elsewhere in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errata handling for books
rubrics_metrics.description: For severe errors detected after printing significant numbers of copies, supply a separate errata page listing corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If copies not yet distributed, errata page may be supplied; errata may be placed at end of front matter or at the end of the book and should be listed in the table of contents; it's now more common to list errata online—publishers who correct electronic versions should include a notice/description of changes and may need to notify readers who received the uncorrected version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothbound cover spine and front/back content
rubrics_metrics.description: On clothbound hardcovers, the spine is generally imprinted with the author's full name (or last name if space is tight), the title (and any edition number), and the publisher’s name; subtitle is usually omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publisher’s name may be shortened or replaced by an emblem; spine copy in American publications is commonly vertical (read from top down), but may be horizontal if space allows; front panel may be blank or bear stamped/printed material; back panel usually blank though a product code may be necessary for books with no jacket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperback cover elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperback spines usually carry author/editor name, publisher name/colophon, and title; front cover carries author/editor name, title, and usually subtitle, sometimes translator or contributor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back cover usually carries promotional copy (description, quotations, author bio), series title if applicable, and sometimes publisher information; paperbacks may include gatefolds (French flaps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dust jacket content and paper-over-board alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Dust jackets on hardcovers include material similar to paperback front and spine and have flaps carrying the remainder of back-cover material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back flap commonly completes promotional copy that begins on the front flap; a paper-over-board (lithocase) allows full-color images and type directly on the cover and inside panels as an alternative to a dust jacket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endpapers description and pagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Endpapers are folded sheets at the beginning and end of a hardcover book; the free half is called a flyleaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endpapers are heavier stock, sometimes printed, and are not counted in a book’s pagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit lines for cover art placement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a credit line is required for artwork on a jacket or cover, it normally appears on the back flap of the jacket or the back cover of a paperback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit for artwork on the actual cover may also appear inside the book (often on the copyright page) since the cover is a permanent part of the bound book; see specific styling guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISBN and bar code placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Book covers need to include ISBN and product/price codes (bar codes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bar codes should appear at the foot of the back cover or dust jacket or any other protective case or wrapper; consult ISBN Agency resources for detailed process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadata core elements and importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Metadata for a book consists of core elements describing the resource: title/subtitle, author and biography, edition, publisher, publication date, ISBN, price, bar code, and a description of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also include cover image, formats, language, extent (page count or duration), subject headings (e.g., BISAC or Thema), keywords, intended audience, availability, and other statistics; enter metadata into publisher databases using standards (e.g., ONIX/XML) to automate product pages and share with libraries/booksellers; accurate complete metadata is essential to a publisher workflow; self-publishing authors are usually required to supply/maintain basic metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts and keywords for books
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts are summaries of a book’s content written by the author and usually limited to a few hundred words or less; publishers may require chapter summaries as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should take care—abstracts often form the basis of promotional copy or descriptive metadata; abstracts may be supplemented by keywords (words/phrases identifying important concepts or names); publishers may ask for keywords for each chapter and the book as whole; keywords improve visibility to search engines and are part of metadata for distribution and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal publication formats and supplementary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly journals are offered in print and electronic formats or electronically only; electronic journals may present content as PDFs (corresponding to print pages) or as full-text HTML with features not in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary data (supporting information) may be published electronically only—large tables, reading lists, multimedia, datasets, color versions of figures, or online-only appendixes; unedited accepted manuscripts ('in press') may be released; any electronic-only materials must be listed in the print version and differences between print and electronic versions must be made apparent in the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISSN and DOI assignment and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals are identified by an ISSN; electronic journals receive a separate ISSN. Articles are identified by page ranges, the Copyright Clearance Center code, and Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A DOI is a unique persistent string that can identify articles and components (tables, figures, multimedia); metadata must clarify components are part of a larger work; append DOI to https://doi.org/ to form persistent links (recommended by Crossref).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal volumes/issues numbering and dating conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal volume usually comprises the issues published in a calendar year (though some use academic year); issues within a volume are typically numbered with arabic numerals starting with 1 each new volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals use cover month/season instead of issue number or number issues consecutively across years; frequency determines the number of issues per volume; some journals publish multiple volumes per year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbering and running heads for journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed journal page numbers usually start with 1 in the volume’s first issue and run continuously to the end of the volume; an issue begins on a right-hand page (recto) and ends on a left-hand page (verso).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic journals with printed counterparts should list corresponding page ranges where they appear (table of contents, article head, citation data); articles published ahead of print may use dummy folios until pagination is finalized; articles not in print can use a separate page-numbering scheme (E1, E2, etc.) running continuously to end of volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous publishing model pagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals assign each article a unique citation ID instead of traditional page ranges to support publication independent of print issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PDF versions are paginated starting with 1 and are cited by citation ID plus page number (e.g., 1234, p.1); such pagination is final and used in print versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running heads/feet content in journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Running heads or feet typically bear the journal title (full or abbreviated), the author’s surname (or shortened author list), the (shortened) article title, or the journal section name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrangement across rectos and versos varies; for full-text scrollable electronic articles, such info may be presented at the head of each article; downloaded articles typically show a URL and date of download in header or footer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal cover panels (1–4) and front matter content
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover 1 (front) displays journal title, volume/issue numbers, date and year, publisher’s name, and sometimes table of contents or illustration; Cover 2 (inside front) usually contains the masthead and editorial information; Cover 3 (inside back) often contains advertising or information for contributors; Cover 4 (back) carries the bar code and may carry table of contents or advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items such as masthead, ISSN, subscription info, copyright line, submission fee notices, indexing info, and statements of editorial policy may appear on cover 2 or in front/back matter; cover panels may be used variably depending on journal design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal home page essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal home page should include essential information such as current volume number and date, table of contents with links to articles, statement of copyright, frequency of publication, and ISSN(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home pages may also provide fuller descriptions of journal and editorial policies, history, links to publisher and society pages, submission instructions and file-prep details, subscription and registration forms, links to past issues, lists of upcoming articles, search engines, indexing/abstracting information, society meeting info, subscriber services, related products, and mail-to contact links for various inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal table of contents elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The table of contents should include the journal title (or special-issue title and editors), date, volume and issue numbers, titles of articles and authors' names, and page range or starting page for each article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may contain section titles and list items like review articles, book reviews, commentaries, and should include articles published electronically only or point readers to the website; electronic TOCs should provide links to each format of each item and include article summaries viewable without subscription; freely available full articles should be labeled; provide options to download citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information for contributors and editorial policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Information for potential contributors varies in length and may include a statement of editorial policy and submission instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short versions may appear in print with pointers to fuller electronic versions for details on preparing and submitting electronic text, tables, math, art, and supplementary files; information can appear on cover panels, front/back matter, or journal website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal errata linking and correction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should publish errata and, for electronic journals, provide two-way links between errata and the articles containing errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles should be updated to link to or indicate the relevant errata; table of contents entries for original articles should also link to errata; small online corrections should be accompanied by a note indicating nature of changes and when they were made.
